title: Desktop app security: CSP, no remote code, narrow native API
when: Review or harden a desktop web app before release, where any script injection could reach the file system or native calls.
inputs: places that render user or file content
prompt: Goal: An app where injected text cannot run, only bundled code runs, and the native bridge exposes only what features need. Steps: 1. CSP meta in every HTML file: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; connect-src 'self' plus exact API hosts; no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval. 2. Move inline handlers and inline scripts into files; no eval, new Function or setTimeout with strings. 3. Load no script from the network; vendor every library into resources/ and pin its version. 4. Render file and user content with textContent or a sanitizer; never innerHTML with untrusted text. 5. nativeAllowList lists exact functions; block os.execCommand, os.spawnProcess and filesystem.remove unless a feature needs them, and then validate every argument. 6. Keep "tokenSecurity": "one-time" and "enableInspector": false in release config; the server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. 7. Never navigate the main window to remote pages; open external links with Neutralino.os.open after checking the scheme is https. 8. Secrets do not belong in resources; anyone can unpack resources.neu. Quality bar: - Each allowed native function maps to a named feature. - A pasted string shows as text. Pitfalls: - Wildcards like "filesystem.*" in the allow list. - Opening links from documents in the app window. Verify: - [ ] CSP meta present without unsafe-inline. - [ ] No eval or remote script tags. - [ ] Allow list has no wildcards. Output: updated HTML heads, neutralino.config.json and SECURITY.md findings.

examples.input: revisa a segurança do meu app desktop antes de publicar
examples.output: Strict CSP meta, vendored scripts, exact allow list without execCommand, inspector off, SECURITY.md
